problem: Existing zero-shot object navigation methods lack persistent, reusable memory (value maps and semantic maps are task-bound or non-persistent; graph memories use object/waypoint nodes in text form), mostly handle a single goal modality, and use greedy planners that cause back-and-forth maneuvers.
motivation: Service robots in lifelong settings should reuse past observations across sequential multimodal goals (image, object, text). Greedy selection of the single most likely frontier ignores the ordering of multiple candidates, wasting path length, while feeding raw global maps to LLMs is unreliable for spatial and long-horizon reasoning.
key_idea: Build a Semantic Skeleton Memory Graph that attaches objects to topological keypoints (junctions and endpoints) of the occupancy-map skeleton, have a VLM estimate target belief per node, and plan a visit order that minimizes expected path length with a 2-opt-style search.
insight: Ablation on a GOAT val_unseen subset shows that memory alone raises SPL (Semantic Map greedy 0.278 vs Value Map greedy 0.258). SSMG with a greedy planner is better still (SPL 0.328), and the long-horizon planner adds more (0.361 without revisiting, 0.376 full). The SPL gains come mainly from persistent skeleton-anchored memory and from planning the visit order, not from better exploration alone. VLFM's lack of improvement over subtask index, versus SSMG-Nav and the RL Monolithic baseline that both improve, further supports the importance of memory.
method: Perception and maps: depth gives a BEV occupancy grid, BLIP-2 gives a target-relevance value map, and Grounding-DINO + MobileSAM + depth produce an object point-cloud map, storing up to K=3 views with captions and scores per object.

Skeleton topology extraction: morphological thinning of the occupancy map yields a medial axis. Only endpoints and junctions are kept as nodes, with connector pixels stored as edge attributes for path planning.

Semantic attachment: each object attaches to the nearest skeleton node via its best-view pose. A data-driven radius per node then adds nearby objects, so an object can belong to several nodes. Endpoints are linked to adjacent junctions.

VLM belief evaluation: per endpoint, a multimodal prompt (object id/class/caption text plus a BEV subgraph image) with CoT goes to Qwen-VL-Plus for a belief score. Endpoint information is then propagated to junctions, and the VLM is queried again for junction belief.

Long-horizon planner: beliefs are turned into probabilities by softmax with temperature. A nearest-neighbour greedy path is refined by 2-opt segment reversal to minimize expected travel cost (NP-hard objective).

Four-stage policy: retrieval from SSMG, revisiting (visit nodes in the planned order with a 360° spin), exploring (frontiers ordered by the same planner using the value map as belief), and waypoint navigation (A* plus the VLFM VER-trained PointNav policy).

setting.backbone: Qwen-VL-Plus (frozen) for belief, BLIP-2, Grounding-DINO, MobileSAM (frozen), plus a pretrained VER PointNav local policy from VLFM
setting.training_data: none (training-free / zero-shot; reuses pretrained models and the VLFM VER policy trained on HM3D)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB 640x480 (79° HFOV) + depth (0.5–5 m) + pose
setting.action_space: low-level: forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 30°, stop (waypoints via A* and a PointNav policy)
setting.simulator: Habitat (GOAT-Bench, HM3D, MP3D); real-world wheeled robot demo
setting.privileged: none (pose is provided by the simulator)

numbers.evidence: Table 1 Lifelong Multimodal Object Navigation Comparison, GOAT val_seen

numbers_note: Metrics printed as fractions (0-1) in the paper and copied as such. Per-modality and per-subtask-index results are only in figures. HM3D/MP3D splits are given without explicit names (standard val), so 'val' is used.
results: On GOAT-Bench SSMG-Nav gets s-SR 0.465 / SPL 0.341 on val_unseen, beating VLFM† (0.406 / 0.159) and Modular GOAT (SPL 0.172) with large SPL gains. On HM3D and MP3D ObjectNav it has the best SPL (0.337, 0.191) with SR comparable to the best baselines (SGM 0.602 and WMNav 0.454 are higher in SR on HM3D and MP3D respectively).
limitations: Relies on large models, causing latency and slow robot velocity in real-world deployment.
e-SR remains very low for all methods, and the real-world validation is only a small qualitative three-subtask demo.
